cases.name: collects reachable rows with $depth
cases.query: id, depth: $depth from tree follow children order by $depth, id

cases.name: depth cap and $stop
cases.query: id, stop: $stop from tree follow children { depth 2 } order by id

cases.name: $leaf and $frontier
cases.query: id, leaf: $leaf, frontier: $frontier, stop: $stop from tree follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: a row without the relation is a leaf
cases.query: id, stop: $stop from xs follow next order by $ordinal

cases.name: $ordinal ranks by depth then path
cases.query: id, o: $ordinal from tree follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: $ordinal path components compare as values
cases.notes: A path is the sequence of identities along the walk; components compare as values (two numbers numerically, two strings by code point), never as joined text — so 9 precedes 10.
cases.query: id values from tree follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: cycles terminate: a revisit is admitted once
cases.notes: Identity is the `id` property; the third row is the revisit of node 1 and is never expanded.
cases.query: id, stop: $stop from g follow next order by $ordinal

cases.name: follow distinct collapses occurrences to nodes
cases.query: id from g follow distinct next order by id

cases.name: a node on two paths yields two occurrences
cases.query: id, d: $depth from g follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: follow distinct keeps one occurrence per identity
cases.query: id, d: $depth from g follow distinct children order by $ordinal

cases.name: by supplies the identity
cases.query: label, stop: $stop from tree follow children { by label } order by $ordinal

cases.name: the hard depth cap is 8
cases.query: id values from c follow next

cases.name: the capped row reports depth
cases.query: id, s: $stop, f: $frontier from c follow next order by $ordinal offset 6

cases.name: frontier cuts a relation that could continue
cases.query: id, s: $stop, f: $frontier, l: $leaf from tree follow children { frontier id == "a" } order by $ordinal

cases.name: where in the follow block filters successors
cases.query: id values from tree follow children { where id != "a" } order by $ordinal

cases.name: top-level where without intrinsics selects seeds
cases.query: id values from tree where id == "a" follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: top-level where with intrinsics filters after the walk
cases.query: id values from tree where $depth > 1 follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: mixed where: seed conjuncts and post conjuncts
cases.notes: `id != "b"` filters seeds only (the root passes); `$depth <= 2` filters the walked occurrences. `b` is reached because seed predicates do not prune the walk.
cases.query: id values from tree where id != "b" && $depth <= 2 follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: intrinsics belong to the reached row; nested blocks read them via ^
cases.query: id, kids: children collect { id, own: $depth, parentDepth: ^$depth } from tree follow children { depth 2 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: follow inside a select-position collect
cases.query: id, desc: children collect { id values follow children order by $ordinal } from tree where id == "root"

cases.name: follow with select distinct
cases.query: select distinct id from g follow next order by id

cases.name: follow is not valid in a where op
cases.query: id from tree where children exists { follow children }

cases.name: depth must be at least 1
cases.query: id from tree follow children { depth 0 }

cases.name: depth must be at most 8
cases.query: id from tree follow children { depth 9 }

cases.name: depth must be an integer
cases.query: id from tree follow children { depth 1.5 }

cases.name: unknown word in the follow block
cases.query: id from tree follow children { foo 1 }

cases.name: duplicate where in the follow block
cases.query: id from tree follow children { where a where b }

cases.name: duplicate depth in the follow block
cases.query: id from tree follow children { depth 1 depth 2 }

cases.name: follow needs a relation
cases.query: from r follow

cases.name: follow over id-less nodes uses structural identity
cases.notes: Without an `id`, identity is the row's structural value; distinct successors are not cycles of each other.
cases.query: n, stop: $stop from t follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: follow identity keeps a number and a numeric string apart
cases.query: id, stop: $stop from t follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: $ordinal path components: numbers precede strings
cases.notes: Components of different kinds do not order by §6; a number component sorts before a string component.
cases.query: id values from t follow children order by $ordinal

cases.name: the follow where reads the frontier row through ^
cases.notes: Inside `follow R { where P }` the candidate's scope hangs off the row being expanded, so `^id` is the parent's id. Before 0.14 `^` skipped to the walk's enclosing scope (the root here), where `id` is absent, and the predicate never held.
cases.query: id values from g follow next { where prev == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: the follow where: a bare name is the candidate's own
cases.query: id values from g follow next { where prev == "z" } order by $ordinal

cases.name: the follow where: ^ is the frontier row inside a nested follow
cases.notes: The collect's rows seed the walk; `^tag` in the follow where is the frontier row's tag (`r1` is `m`), not the enclosing row's.
cases.query: id, desc: kids collect { id values follow kids { where tag == ^tag } order by $ordinal } from t

cases.name: the follow where: ^^ is the walk's enclosing scope
cases.notes: Two carets out of the follow where is the scope the walk runs in — here the enclosing `root` row (tag `k`).
cases.query: id, desc: kids collect { id values follow kids { where tag == ^^tag } order by $ordinal } from t

cases.name: frontier and by read the occurrence with ^ the enclosing scope
cases.notes: `frontier`/`by` are not correlated: `^tag` there is the enclosing `root` row's tag (`k`), so `r1b` and `r2` are frontiers and `r1` (`m`) expands.
cases.query: id, desc: kids collect { id, s: $stop follow kids { frontier tag == ^tag } order by $ordinal } from t

cases.name: two destinations walk their union
cases.query: id, d: $depth from g follow before, after order by $ordinal

cases.name: destinations are unioned by identity within a step
cases.notes: Node 2 is both `before` and `after` of node 1; one step yields it once.
cases.query: id, d: $depth from g follow before, after order by $ordinal

cases.name: a relation holding a node twice yields one successor
cases.notes: The within-step union applies to a single destination too (since 0.14).
cases.query: id, d: $depth from t follow kids order by $ordinal

cases.name: a row lacking one destination still follows the others
cases.query: id values from g follow before, after order by $ordinal

cases.name: the options block applies to the union: depth
cases.query: id, s: $stop from g follow before, after { depth 2 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: the options block applies to the union: where
cases.query: id values from g follow before, after { where id != 3 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: frontier applies to a row whichever destination reached it
cases.query: id, s: $stop from g follow before, after { frontier id == 3 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: follow distinct over two destinations
cases.query: id, d: $depth from g follow distinct before, after order by $ordinal

cases.name: a destination block computes successors per frontier row
cases.notes: `^people` is read in the frontier row's scope, one out of which is the root; inside the block `^id` is the frontier row's id. The walk is the reporting tree under person 1.
cases.query: id values from people where id == 1 follow ^people collect { where manager == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a destination block's projection shapes the successors
cases.notes: The block projects `{ id }`, so every walked row after the seed carries only `id`; `manager` is absent on them.
cases.query: id, m: manager from people where id == 1 follow ^people collect { id where manager == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: first as a destination yields at most one successor
cases.query: id values from people where id == 1 follow ^people first { where manager == ^id order by id desc } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a destination block honors its own limit
cases.query: id values from people where id == 1 follow ^people collect { where manager == ^id order by id limit 1 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a relation and a block walk both directions of a chain
cases.notes: Predecessors come from the frontier row's `prev` looked up in the root; successors are the rows whose `prev` names the frontier row. Each neighbour steps back onto the seed, admitted once as a cycle.
cases.query: id, s: $stop from chain where id == "b" follow ^chain collect { where id == ^prev }, ^chain collect { where prev == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: follow distinct over a bidirectional chain walk
cases.query: id values from chain where id == "b" follow distinct ^chain collect { where id == ^prev }, ^chain collect { where prev == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a destination block inside a nested follow correlates with the frontier row
cases.notes: Inside the block `^id` is the frontier row (the walked person), `^^id` would be the enclosing `teams` row.
cases.query: id, chain: people collect { id values where id == ^lead follow ^people collect { where manager == ^id } order by $ordinal } from teams

cases.name: a trailing comma needs another destination
cases.query: id from tree follow children, { depth 2 }

cases.name: a comma at the end of the query needs another destination
cases.query: id from tree follow children,

cases.name: a later plain destination does not take an outer reference
cases.query: id from tree follow children, ^others

cases.name: a literal is not a later destination
cases.query: id from tree follow children, null

cases.name: a destination block must use collect/first/single
cases.query: id from tree follow ^tree exists { where parent == ^id }

cases.name: a destination block must use collect/first/single: count
cases.query: id from tree follow children count { }

cases.name: a destination block is closed before the options block
cases.query: id from tree follow ^tree collect { where parent == ^id } { depth 2

includes: expected '}' to close the follow block

cases.name: an outer-reference destination with a brace is a destination block (implicit collect)
cases.notes: Since 0.19 a receiver headed by an outer reference can never be a plain destination, so its brace opens a destination block — `^docs { … }` ≡ `^docs collect { … }` — not the options block. `^path` inside the block is the frontier row's path: the walk reaches every document whose `after` names the row being expanded.
cases.query: path values from docs where path == "/p/kickoff" follow ^docs { where ^path in list(after) } order by $ordinal

cases.name: an outer-reference destination block may lead with its predicate (where-first)
cases.notes: The 0.17 body rules apply inside the block: a leading `in` predicate opens a `where`-first body.
cases.query: path values from docs where path == "/p/kickoff" follow ^docs { ^path in list(after) } order by $ordinal

cases.name: an outer-reference destination block projects its successors
cases.notes: A projection inside the block shapes the walked rows like any destination block, and the projected records are what gets expanded next — so the projection keeps `path`, which the block reads through `^path` at the following step. The seed keeps its own shape.
cases.query: title, d: $depth from docs where id == 1 follow ^docs { title, path where ^path in list(after) } order by $ordinal

cases.name: an absolute-reference destination with a brace is a destination block
cases.notes: `0^docs` is `^docs` from a top-level walk (the receiver is read in the frontier row's scope, depth 1); inside the block (depth 2) `1^path` is `^path`, the frontier row.
cases.query: path values from docs where id == 1 follow 0^docs { where 1^path in list(after) } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a two-caret destination with a brace is a destination block inside a nested collect's follow
cases.notes: The nested block's rows are depth 2, so `^^people` read in the frontier row's scope is the root; inside the destination block `^id` is the frontier row (the walked person) and `^^lead` would be the team row.
cases.query: id, chain: ^people collect { id values where id == ^lead follow ^^people { where manager == ^id } order by $ordinal } from teams

cases.name: a member chain over an outer reference with a brace is a destination block
cases.notes: The rule is about the receiver's head: `^$it.people` is an outer reference with a member chain, so its brace is a destination block.
cases.query: id values from people where id == 1 follow ^$it.people { where manager == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: an options block after a trailing destination block (implicit collect)
cases.notes: The brace right after `^people` is the block; the brace after the block's `}` is the options block, as it has been since 0.14 for an explicit consumer.
cases.query: id, s: $stop from people where id == 1 follow ^people { where manager == ^id } { depth 2 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: an options block after a trailing destination block (explicit collect)
cases.query: id, s: $stop from people where id == 1 follow ^people collect { where manager == ^id } { depth 2 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: the options where applies on top of a destination block's own where
cases.query: id values from people where id == 1 follow ^people { where manager == ^id } { where id != 3 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: two destinations: a plain relation and an outer-reference block, unioned by identity
cases.notes: Both destinations reach `b` from `a` (the nested `kids` row and the root row share the identity `b`); one step keeps it once. From that `b` only the block finds `c`.
cases.query: id values from nodes where id == "a" follow kids, ^nodes { where parent == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: two outer-reference blocks walk both directions of a chain (implicit collect)
cases.notes: The implicit-collect spelling of "a relation and a block walk both directions of a chain".
cases.query: id values from chain where id == "b" follow distinct ^chain { where id == ^prev }, ^chain { where prev == ^id } order by $ordinal

cases.name: the options where after an explicit destination block
cases.notes: Pinned alongside the implicit form: the second brace after `^chain collect { … }` is the options block, as it has been since 0.14.
cases.query: id values from chain where id == "a" follow ^chain collect { where prev == ^id } { where id != "c" } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a brace after a plain destination of several is still the options block
cases.notes: `children` is the last destination and a relation of the current row, so `{ depth 2 }` caps the walk (it is not a block).
cases.query: id, s: $stop from tree follow a, children { depth 2 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a brace after a free-function destination is the options block: depth
cases.notes: A call receiver (`entries(kids)`) is read in the current row, so its brace is the options block, like a bare relation's.
cases.query: id, s: $stop from tree follow entries(kids) { depth 2 } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a brace after a free-function destination is the options block: where
cases.query: id values from tree follow entries(kids) { where id != "a" } order by $ordinal

cases.name: a predicate in the brace after a plain destination of several is the options error
cases.notes: `children` is a relation of the current row, so its brace is the options block; the message says a destination block needs its consumer.
cases.query: id from tree follow a, children { id != "root" }

includes: a destination block needs its consumer

cases.name: a plain outer-reference destination is an error naming the block spellings
cases.notes: No brace and no consumer: `^children` cannot be a relation of the current row. The message offers both block spellings.
cases.query: id from tree follow ^children

walks a root collection only as a destination block

cases.name: a destination block over an outer reference still rejects exists
cases.query: id from tree follow ^tree exists { parent == ^id }

cases.name: an implicit destination block is closed before the options block
cases.query: id from tree follow ^tree { where parent == ^id } { depth 2
